entrepreneur.intro: Learn to start, run, and grow a business in West Africa. From spotting opportunities to managing cash flow to scaling.

skillDomains.name: Opportunity
skillDomains.description: Find problems worth solving and prove they're worth money.

skills.name: Spotting Opportunity
skills.description: Train your eye to see business ideas in daily problems.

modules.title: Where ideas come from
modules.content:
Business ideas don't come from inspiration. They come from noticing problems.

The three sources

  1. Frustration — what annoys you or people around you repeatedly?
  2. Inefficiency — what takes longer or costs more than it should?
  3. Change — what's new (tech, regulation, migration, weather patterns)?

West African examples

  • Long fuel queues → fuel delivery service
  • Slow mobile money floats → float top-up service
  • Expensive imported food → local packaging and processing
  • Youth unemployment → training and placement agency

modules.title: Frame the problem, not the solution
modules.content:
Beginners pitch solutions: "I want to start a restaurant."

Entrepreneurs pitch problems: "Office workers in my area have nowhere to eat lunch quickly and cheaply."

Why it matters

The problem stays stable. The solution can change. If your restaurant fails, you pivot to a lunch delivery service — the problem is still there.

Try it

Instead of "I want to open a shop", say "People in this neighbourhood can't easily buy X". Then ask: who exactly? How many? What do they do now instead?

steps.q: Which of these is a well-framed business idea?
o: Women in my district can't find affordable work-appropriate blouses

steps.q: A market has 3 phone repair shops already. Should you open another?
o: Only if you can offer something they don't (speed, price, location, guarantee)

steps.q: You notice your neighbourhood has no laundry service. What's your first step?
o: Talk to 20 potential customers about whether they'd use it and pay for it
steps.f: Customer conversations before any spending. Always.

skills.name: Customer Discovery
skills.description: Talk to customers in a way that reveals truth, not politeness.

modules.title: Ask about the past, not the future
modules.content:
People are nice. If you ask "would you buy this?", they'll say yes. Then they won't.

Ask about real behaviour

  • Bad: Would you buy a home delivery service?
  • Good: How did you get your last meal? How much did it cost? How long did it take?

The past is data. The future is a guess.

The five questions

  1. What problem do you have with X?
  2. How do you currently handle it?
  3. What does it cost you (money, time, stress)?
  4. What have you tried before?
  5. What would make you switch?

steps.q: Which question gives the most useful data?
o: Would you use a cleaning service?
How do you currently clean your house and how much time does it take?

steps.q: A customer says "that sounds like a great idea!" What do you do?
o: Ask what specifically they'd use it for and how often

steps.q: You're getting the same complaint from 10 different people. What does it mean?
o: Strong signal — this is a real problem
steps.f: Repeated pain points are the strongest validation signal there is.

skillDomains.name: Operations
skillDomains.description: Deliver consistently. Operations is what turns a sale into a business.

modules.title: Everything is a process
modules.content:
Every task in a business can be written as a process:

  1. What triggers it?
  2. What are the steps?
  3. Who does each step?
  4. What quality check happens?
  5. How long should it take?

Why it matters

Written processes:

  • Let you hire and train people quickly
  • Prevent inconsistency
  • Reveal where time and money leak
  • Make the business sellable later

A business that only runs on the founder's memory can't grow.

modules.title: Design a simple process
modules.prompt: You run a small bakery. Orders come in through WhatsApp. You're hiring your first employee. Write out the standard process for handling a customer order from first message to delivery.
modules.context: Documented processes are how a one-person operation becomes a business.
rubric: Defines what triggers the process (customer message)
Lists each step clearly in order
Assigns responsibility (who does what)
Includes a cost and time estimate
Includes a quality check before delivery
Defines what to do if something goes wrong
Includes confirmation with customer at key points

skillDomains.name: Finance
skillDomains.description: Money is the language of business. Learn to speak it.

skills.name: Cash Flow
skills.description: Track money in and money out. Most businesses die from cash problems, not profit problems.

modules.title: Profit is not cash
modules.content:
A business can be profitable and still fail. Here's how:

You sell 100 bags of rice on credit. Your books show 500,000 Le profit. But you haven't been paid yet, and you owe your supplier 400,000 Le today. You can't pay. The business dies.

The golden rule

Track cash flow weekly. Not monthly. Not yearly. Weekly.

Three numbers

  • Cash on hand (money in bank and drawer)
  • Cash coming in next 30 days
  • Cash going out next 30 days

If (in + on hand) < out, you have a problem.

steps.q: You have 100,000 Le cash. You owe supplier 80,000 Le this week and have rent 40,000 Le due next week. What do you do?
o: Pay supplier fully, negotiate rent delay, and push for customer payments
steps.f: Protect the supplier relationship. Negotiate rent. Get customer money in.

steps.q: A big customer wants 60-day payment terms. Your normal is 14 days. What do you consider?
o: Calculate the cash cost of waiting 60 days and price accordingly

steps.q: You're profitable but can't make payroll. What's the most likely cause?
o: Cash tied up in inventory or receivables
steps.f: Profit locked in stock or unpaid invoices can't pay salaries.

skills.name: Pricing
skills.description: Price for the business to survive and grow.

modules.title: The four-part price
modules.content:
Every price must cover:

  1. Cost of goods — what you buy or make the product for
  2. Labour — your time and your staff's time
  3. Overhead — rent, transport, electricity, marketing
  4. Margin — profit that grows the business

Common mistake

New entrepreneurs price at "cost + a little". This leaves no room for anything.

The formula

Price = (COGS + Labour + Overhead) × (1 + Margin)

Standard margins: retail 30-50%, services 40-70%, food 60-70%.

modules.title: Price a product line
modules.prompt: You're launching a line of packaged groundnut paste (peanut butter) for local sale. Ingredients cost 800 Le per jar. Packaging costs 300 Le. Labour is 200 Le per jar. Overhead is 150 Le per jar. What do you charge, and how do you think about it?

skillDomains.name: Sales & Marketing
skillDomains.description: Get the word out. Get the cash in.

skills.name: Sales
skills.description: Convince people to buy. This is not a dirty word.

modules.title: Sales is service
modules.content:
Sales is not manipulation. It is helping someone decide to solve a problem they have.

The sales conversation

  1. Ask — what problem do they have?
  2. Listen — don't interrupt. Let them talk.
  3. Match — connect your product to their stated problem
  4. Prove — show evidence: testimonials, demo, sample
  5. Ask — for the sale. Directly. "Shall I deliver on Monday?"

Most sales fail at step 5 — the salesperson never actually asks for the sale.

steps.q: A potential customer says "it's too expensive". Best response?
o: Ask what they're comparing it to, then address the value
Say the price is the price
steps.f: Expensive compared to what? Find the comparison, then re-frame the value.

steps.q: You've given your pitch and the customer is silent. What do you do?
o: Ask a question to understand their concern

steps.q: A customer says "let me think about it". What's your best move?
o: Ask what specifically they're considering, and offer to follow up on a specific day
steps.f: "Let me think" is often a soft no.

skills.name: Marketing
skills.description: Reach people who don't know you yet.

modules.title: Marketing channels that work in West Africa
modules.content:
WhatsApp Business

The single most important tool. Post updates, catalogue products, respond to enquiries. Free and effective.

Instagram and TikTok

Visual products thrive. Consistent posting of quality photos builds a following.

Word of mouth

Still the #1 channel. Ask happy customers to refer. Reward referrals.

Radio

Still strong outside major cities. Local-language radio reaches large audiences.

Community events

Markets, churches, mosques, schools. Be present where your customers already are.

modules.title: Build a marketing plan
modules.prompt: You've launched a small juice business selling fresh juice to offices. You have 20,000 Le per month for marketing. Describe how you'd spend it.
rubric: Prioritises WhatsApp Business (free or low cost)
Uses in-person sampling at nearby offices
Uses modest paid promotion on one platform, not many
Asks for referrals from first customers
Tracks which channel brings actual sales
Keeps the budget under 20,000 Le

skillDomains.name: Scaling
skillDomains.description: From one person to a team to a real company.

skills.name: Hiring
skills.description: Find, train, and keep good people.

modules.title: Your first hire
modules.content:
The first hire is the hardest. You're handing over part of your business to someone you don't know.

Look for

  • Reliability over skill — you can teach skill, you can't teach reliability
  • Attitude — how they handle frustration matters more than how they interview
  • Proven work — ask for references and actually call them
  • Cultural fit — will they represent your business well?

Test before you commit

Hire for a trial period. One month. Both sides learn whether it works.

modules.title: Write a job ad
modules.prompt: You run a growing tailoring business. You need a full-time assistant. Write a job advertisement for WhatsApp and Facebook.
modules.context: Well-written job ads attract serious applicants.
rubric: States the role clearly (tailoring assistant)
States working hours and location
States pay range
Lists required skills and attitude
Asks for a specific response (send photo of your work)
Includes a filter that weeds out non-serious applicants
